summary:
We developed FlameWatch through Replit, it’s an interactive research simulation that explores how gravity, oxygen concentration, airflow, and fuel materials affect fire behavior. The platform allows users to adjust different environmental conditions and observe how a flame changes, including the formation of spherical flames under microgravity conditions.
FlameWatch addresses the challenge of understanding complex combustion behavior by providing a visual and interactive learning experience. Instead of relying only on theoretical explanations, users can experiment with different parameters and observe their effects on flame characteristics and combustion risk. This project is important because it promotes awareness of fire behavior, supports scientific learning, and helps users understand how environmental factors influence combustion. It also demonstrates how interactive technology can make complex scientific concepts easier to explore and understand.
details:
FlameWatch: Making Space Fire Research Accessible

FlameWatch is an interactive educational platform designed to help people understand how fire behaves in the unique conditions of space. Built as a web-based simulation, it allows users to adjust key environmental factors such as gravity, oxygen concentration, airflow, and fuel type, and immediately observe how these changes affect flame shape and behavior. The tool draws directly on decades of NASA combustion research, including experiments such as BASS/BASS-II, Saffire, and FLEX, which studied solid-fuel burning, fire spread in uncrewed spacecraft, and the persistence of combustion after a visible flame disappears.

At its core, FlameWatch translates complex scientific findings into a hands-on experience. In microgravity, for example, the absence of buoyancy causes flames to form more spherical shapes rather than the familiar teardrop form seen on Earth. Introducing even modest airflow can stretch the flame and supply fresh oxygen, altering its behavior in ways that are difficult to grasp from technical papers alone. By letting users experiment with these variables in real time, the platform turns abstract research into something tangible and memorable.

The benefits of this approach are clear. Traditional NASA data on space fire safety often remains buried in technical databases, inaccessible to students, educators, and even many engineers. FlameWatch lowers that barrier. It demonstrates that oxygen level alone is not a reliable indicator of safety. Pressure, airflow, and fuel properties all play critical roles. It also highlights an important caution from the research: the disappearance of a visible flame does not always mean combustion has stopped. These insights help users develop a more nuanced understanding of fire hazards in spacecraft, lunar habitats, and future Mars bases.

The intended impact of the project is both educational and practical. As humanity prepares for longer missions beyond low Earth orbit, fire safety becomes a life-critical concern. By making NASA’s findings interactive and approachable, FlameWatch aims to raise awareness among the next generation of scientists, engineers, and mission planners. The goal is not to replace rigorous engineering analysis, but to foster informed curiosity and a deeper appreciation of the challenges involved in keeping crews safe.

Developed primarily on Replit, FlameWatch is a browser-based application that requires no specialized hardware. Users interact through a clean interface featuring adjustable settings, dynamic visualizations, and curated summaries of relevant NASA studies. The underlying model is deliberately qualitative rather than a full computational fluid dynamics simulation. This choice prioritizes clarity and accessibility while still remaining grounded in real experimental findings.

What makes FlameWatch creative is its ability to bridge the gap between dense scientific literature and intuitive learning. Instead of presenting static diagrams or lengthy reports, it offers an immediate feedback loop. Change a parameter and watch the flame respond. The progressive presentation of NASA experiments, beginning with prevention, moving to fire spread, and then to suppression, further guides users through the research in a logical sequence. Strong, repeated disclaimers ensure that the tool is never mistaken for a predictive safety system, maintaining scientific integrity while encouraging exploration.

In designing the platform, the team carefully balanced several competing priorities. Scientific accuracy had to be preserved without overwhelming non-experts. Accessibility was essential, yet the tool could not oversimplify the physics to the point of misleading users. Clear communication of limitations was prioritized so that no one would treat the simulation as a real risk-assessment tool. Finally, the selection of variables focused on those most relevant to space environments (gravity, oxygen, airflow, and fuel) while acknowledging that certain settings, such as partial gravity on the Moon or Mars, serve as illustrative models rather than exact experimental results.

In short, FlameWatch demonstrates how interactive technology can make specialized research more approachable. By turning NASA’s microgravity combustion studies into a living, adjustable experience, it helps users see why fire behaves differently in space and why those differences matter for the future of human exploration.
